demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette: Akua had always been close to her younger brother, Kwame. Growing up in a tight-knit Ghanaian family in the United States, they shared everything from their deepest secrets to their wildest dreams. So when Kwame died suddenly in a car accident, Akua's world was shattered. She was consumed by an overwhelming sense of guilt and self-blame, repeatedly replaying the what-ifs in her mind: "If only I had been more careful, if only I had warned him about the dangers of driving at night." These thoughts morphed into a pervasive feeling that she was somehow responsible for his death. As time passed, Akua found herself increasingly irritable and quick to anger. She would pick arguments with friends and family, creating drama as a way to distract herself from the crushing weight of her grief. But even these distractions couldn't shake off the constant threat she felt lurking in every corner. When things didn't go according to plan, she assumed something bad was happening - her mind racing with worst-case scenarios. Her body would react before her mind had time to catch up, leaving her breathless and on edge. Akua struggled to recall the details of that fateful night, pushing the memories away before they could fully form in her mind. When she tried to talk about it, she found herself unable to find the words - as if the trauma had stolen not just her brother but also her voice. The memory felt like it was happening right now, rather than something that was over and done with. She would see Kwame's smile in crowds, only to realize it was someone else. Akua couldn't help but feel that what happened to her was deeply unfair - a gross injustice that had been left unaddressed. She became convinced that others would have handled the situation better, that they would have somehow prevented the accident. This sense of inadequacy bled into every aspect of her life, making her question her own character and worth. As an environmental scientist, Akua was used to being in control, but now she felt like a tiny boat adrift in a stormy sea. As the months went by, these feelings of inadequacy and injustice began to shape Akua's behavior. She became increasingly avoidant, steering clear of TV shows or films that dealt with similar themes - unable to bear the thought of reliving her own trauma through someone else's story. Her sleep problems worsened, leaving her exhausted and irritable. One particularly grueling day at work, as she struggled to meet a looming deadline, Akua felt like everything was conspiring against her. She snapped at a colleague, lashing out in frustration - another instance of seeking conflict to distract herself from the pain that lingered beneath the surface. But even this momentary distraction couldn't erase the feeling that something bad was waiting just around the corner. It was this constant sense of threat that finally brought Akua to seek help. She realized she couldn't keep living like this - perpetually on edge, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. What frightened her most was losing herself completely in this sea of grief and guilt, never finding a way back to the person she once was. As she sat in her therapist's office, Akua knew it wouldn't be easy, but she was ready to confront the memories and emotions that had been holding her hostage for so long.
